newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Last flutter for S.Africa's rare Brenton Blue.
newsitem.headline: Last flutter for S.Africa's rare Brenton Blue.

text.p: Time is running out for the Brenton Blue -- a tiny South African butterfly which appears doomed for living at a beach holiday resort.
The Brenton Blue lives in a small spot on the country's south coast which developers want to bulldoze for holiday homes.

"For the first time in our history, we are about to knowingly allow a species of life to be exterminated by human greed without raising a finger to stop it," legislator Errol Moorcroft told Reuters on Wednesday.

The site at Brenton-on-Sea, near the renowned Knysna Lagoon which draws thousands of foreign and local tourists every year, is the last known habitat of the once plentiful Brenton Blue, which was first identified in 1855.

The site is valued at around 1.6 million rand ($360,000) and, at the peak of their season, is home to around 300 of the butterflies, which rely on a particular species of heather and a particular ant to complete their unique life cycle.

Moorcroft urged Environment Minister Pallo Jordan to act before a developer's moratorium expires at the end of the month and the Brenton Blue's half-hectare (one acre) home is taken over by its new owners.
Activist Conrad Steenkamp said he hoped Jordan would step in to save the rare insect, which happens to have the same taste as humans when it comes to choosing a coastal home.
"If he does not take any action we will have to examine our options," Steenkamp said.
"Like people, the Brenton Blue likes wind-still plots about a kilometre (mile) from the sea. That's its problem."
Moorcroft said Jordan could invoke environment protection legislation to save the Benton Blue, buying the land for a reserve or encouraging a swap for state land of equivalent value.
